The nonlinear 2D supercritical inviscid shallow water equations in a rectangle

Aimin Huang , Madalina Petcu and Roger Temam Address: The Institute for Scientific Computing and Applied Mathematics, Indiana University, 831 East Third Street, Rawles Hall, Bloomington, Indiana 47405, U.S.A. Address: Laboratoire de Mathématiques et applications, Univ. de Poitiers, Teleport 2-BP 30179, Boulevard Marie et Pierre Curie, 86962 Futuroscope Chasseneuil Cedex, France Email address: AH:huangepn@gmail.com Email address: MP:Madalina.Petcu@math.univ-poitiers.fr Email address: RT:temam@indiana.edu
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

In this article we consider the inviscid two-dimensional shallow water equations in a rectangle. The flow occurs near a stationary solution in the so called supercritical regime and we establish short term existence of smooth solutions for the corresponding initial and boundary value problem.

Key words and phrases: 
Shallow water equations, inviscid flow, initial and boundary value problems

1. Introduction

Motivated by the study of the inviscid primitive equations, we consider in this article the inviscid two-dimensional shallow water equations in a rectangle in the so-called supercritical regime. It has been shown that a certain vertical expansion of the inviscid primitive equations leads to a system of coupled nonlinear equations similar to the inviscid shallow water equations; see [RTT08b] and [HT14a]. Hence beside their intrinsic interest, the nonlinear shallow water equations can be seen as one mode of the vertical expansion of the primitive equations.

The issue of the boundary conditions to be associated with the primitive or shallow water equations has been emphasized as a major problem and limitation for the so-called Local Area Models for which weather predictions are sought and simulations are performed within a domain for which the boundary has no physical significance, so that there are no physical laws prescribing the boundary conditions (see [WPT97] and e.g. [RTT08a, RTT08b], [CSTT12, SLTT]). The choice of the boundary conditions relies then on mathematical considerations (derivation of a well-posed mathematical problem), and on general computational considerations and physical intuition. The boundary conditions suitable for the one-dimensional shallow water equations were derived in an intuitive context in the book of Whitham [Whi99] and in [NHF08]; see [PT13] for a rigorous study. For general results on boundary value problems for quasilinear hyperbolic system in space dimension one see [LY85]; for initial and boundary value problems for hyperbolic equations in smooth domain see the thorough book [BS07]. The present article follows the study of the one-dimensional inviscid shallow water equations in [PT13, HPT11] and the study of the linearized shallow water equations in [HT14a]. In the study of the linearized inviscid shallow water equations in [HT14a] we have shown that five cases can occur depending on the respective values of the velocity and the height (not counting the non-generic cases and the symmetries). The nonlinear case that we consider in this article relates to what was called the supercritical case in [HT14a]; see [HT14b] for the study of a subcritical case.

In this article, we consider the inviscid fully nonlinear 2D shallow water equations (SWE)

(1.1) {ut+u​ux+v​uy+g​ϕx−f​v=0,vt+u​vx+v​vy+g​ϕy+f​u=0,ϕt+u​ϕx+v​ϕy+ϕ⁡(ux+vy)=0;\begin{cases}u_{t}+uu_{x}+vu_{y}+g\phi_{x}-fv=0,\\ v_{t}+uv_{x}+vv_{y}+g\phi_{y}+fu=0,\\ \phi_{t}+u\phi_{x}+v\phi_{y}+\phi(u_{x}+v_{y})=0;\end{cases}

here U=(u,v,ϕ)t,(x,y)∈Ω:=(0,L1)×(0,L2),t∈(0,T)U=(u,v,\phi)^{t},(x,y)\in\Omega:=(0,L_{1})\times(0,L_{2}),t\in(0,T), uu and vv are the two horizontal components of the velocity, ϕ\phi is the height of the water, and gg is the gravitational acceleration, ff is the Coriolis parameter. The first and second equations (1.1) are derived from the equations of conservation of horizontal momentum, and the third one expresses the conservation of mass. We consider equations (1.1) for certain values of u,v,ϕu,v,\phi as described below, corresponding to a ”supercritical” flow and we associate with (1.1), initial conditions for u,v,ϕu,v,\phi and boundary conditions at x=0x=0 and y=0y=0, u,v,ϕu,v,\phi vanishing on that part of the boundary.

This article is organized as follows. After this introductory section, we derive in Section 2 suitable density theorems, density of certain smooth functions in certain function spaces of Sobolev type. Section 3 is devoted to the modified (symmetrized) SWE operator for the time-independent and the time-dependent cases. It prepares Section 4 in which we deal with the linear SWE, linearized around a non-constant time-dependent flow unlike in [HT14a] where the background flow is time-independent. In Section 4 we prove the well-posedness of the linearized SWE at the price of a loss of derivatives (see Theorem 4.1), and then the well-posedness of the linearized SWE in a short time without a loss of derivatives (see Theorem 4.2). Section 5 considers the fully nonlinear SWE, for which the local well-posedness result is obtained. In the Appendices A and B, we collect some useful theorems about semigroup and evolution systems, and several classical estimates about functions in Sobolev spaces.

2. The density theorems

In this section, we establish general density theorems for certain Sobolev spaces; the results supplement and complement those of Section 3 in [HT14a] which we recall when needed. These theorems have independent interest, and also will be needed for proving later on that −A-A generates a quasi-contraction semigroup on certain Sobolev spaces, where AA is the 2D modified SWE operator associated with suitable boundary conditions.

Proposition 2.3 (A trace theorem).

Proof.

Since θ∈L2​(Ω)\theta\in L^{2}(\Omega), we see that θy\theta_{y} belongs to Lx2​(0,L1,Hy−1​(0,L2))L_{x}^{2}(0,L_{1};H_{y}^{-1}(0,L_{2})), which implies that λ​θx\lambda\theta_{x} belongs to Lx2​(0,L1,Hy−1​(0,L2))L_{x}^{2}(0,L_{1};H_{y}^{-1}(0,L_{2})) by observing that T​θ=λ​θx+θy∈L2​(Ω)T\theta=\lambda\theta_{x}+\theta_{y}\in L^{2}(\Omega). Using assumptions (2.1) and (2.2) when m=0m=0 for λ\lambda, we obtain θx∈Lx2​(0,L1,Hy−1​(0,L2))\theta_{x}\in L_{x}^{2}(0,L_{1};H_{y}^{-1}(0,L_{2})), which, in combination with θ∈Lx2​(0,L1,Ly2​(0,L2))\theta\in L_{x}^{2}(0,L_{1};L_{y}^{2}(0,L_{2})), shows that θ∈𝒞x​([0,L1],Hy−1​(0,L2))\theta\in\mathcal{C}_{x}([0,L_{1}];H_{y}^{-1}(0,L_{2})). Note that when m=0m=0, the space ℋ𝚪0​(Ω)\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{0}(\Omega) is the space L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega).

We first have the following characterizations for the space 𝒳𝚪m​(Ω)\mathcal{X}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}(\Omega).

Proposition 2.4.

For all integer m≥0m\geq 0, we have

𝒳𝚪m(Ω)={θ∈ℋ𝚪m(Ω):Tθ∈ℋ𝚪m(Ω),∂αθ|𝚪=0,∀|α|=m};\mathcal{X}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}(\Omega)=\{\theta\in\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}(\Omega)\,:\,T\theta\in\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}(\Omega),\,\partial^{\alpha}\theta\big|_{{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}}=0,\,\forall\,|\alpha|=m\};

for all integer m≥1m\geq 1, we have

(2.18) 𝒳𝚪m​(Ω)={θ∈ℋ𝚪m​(Ω):T​θ∈ℋ𝚪m​(Ω)}.\mathcal{X}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}(\Omega)=\{\theta\in\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}(\Omega)\,:\,T\theta\in\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}(\Omega)\}.
Proof.

It is clear that the first statement holds for m=0m=0, we thus only need to show the second statement. By definition of the spaces ℋ𝚪m​(Ω)\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}(\Omega) and 𝒳𝚪m​(Ω)\mathcal{X}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}(\Omega), we see that

In order to prove the converse inclusion, let θ\theta belongs to the right-hand side of (2.18), then it is clear that we only need to show that θ\theta satisfies the boundary conditions ∂αθ|𝚪=0\partial^{\alpha}\theta\big|_{{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}}=0 for all |α|=m|\alpha|=m. Furthermore, we only need to show that

(2.19) ∂xmθ|Γ1=0, and ​∂ymθ|Γ2=0,\partial_{x}^{m}\theta|_{\Gamma_{1}}=0,\text{ and }\,\partial_{y}^{m}\theta|_{\Gamma_{2}}=0,

since the other boundary conditions involve the derivatives with respect to tangential directions. Since T​θ∈ℋ𝚪m​(Ω)T\theta\in\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}(\Omega), on Γ1={x=0}\Gamma_{1}=\{x=0\}, we have

(2.20) 0=∂xm−1(λ​θx+θy)=∑k=0m−1∂xm−k−1(λ⁡(x,y))​∂xkθx+∂xm−1θy+λ​∂xmθ,0=\partial_{x}^{m-1}(\lambda\theta_{x}+\theta_{y})=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\partial_{x}^{m-k-1}(\lambda(x,y))\partial_{x}^{k}\theta_{x}+\partial_{x}^{m-1}\theta_{y}+\lambda\partial_{x}^{m}\theta,

which, together with θ∈ℋ𝚪m​(Ω)\theta\in\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}(\Omega), implies that λ​∂xmθ=0\lambda\partial_{x}^{m}\theta=0. We thus have ∂xmθ=0\partial_{x}^{m}\theta=0 on Γ1\Gamma_{1}. Similarly, we can also show that ∂ymθ=0\partial_{y}^{m}\theta=0 on Γ2\Gamma_{2}. We thus completed the proof.

∎

As an immediate consequence of Proposition 2.1, we also find the following equivalent characterizations of the space 𝒳𝚪m​(Ω)\mathcal{X}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}(\Omega).

Proposition 2.5.
𝒳𝚪m​(Ω)={θ∈Hm(Ω):T∂αθ∈L2(Ω),∀|α|=m;∂αθ|𝚪=0,∀|α|≤m}={θ∈ℋ𝚪m(Ω):T∂αθ∈L2(Ω),∂αθ|𝚪=0,∀|α|=m}.\begin{split}\mathcal{X}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}(\Omega)&=\{\theta\in H^{m}(\Omega)\,:\,T\partial^{\alpha}\theta\in L^{2}(\Omega),\,\forall\,|\alpha|=m;\,\partial^{\alpha}\theta\big|_{{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}}=0,\,\forall\,|\alpha|\leq m\}\\ &=\{\theta\in\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}(\Omega)\,:\,T\partial^{\alpha}\theta\in L^{2}(\Omega),\,\partial^{\alpha}\theta\big|_{{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}}=0,\,\forall\,|\alpha|=m\}.\end{split}

Recall that 𝚪=Γ1∪Γ3={x=0}∪{y=0}{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}=\Gamma_{1}\cup\Gamma_{3}=\{x=0\}\cup\{y=0\}, and then we state the density theorems:

Theorem 2.1.

𝒱𝚪​(Ω)∩ℋ𝚪m​(Ω)\mathcal{V}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}(\Omega)\cap\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}(\Omega) is dense in ℋ𝚪m​(Ω)\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}(\Omega).

Theorem 2.2.

Suppose that λ=λ⁡(x,y)\lambda=\lambda(x,y) satisfies the positive mm-condition. Then we have

Theorem 2.2 considers the density of the function space 𝒳𝚪m​(Ω)\mathcal{X}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}(\Omega) involving functions like T​θT\theta, hence this result is not included in Theorem 2.1.

The proof of Theorem 2.1 is similar to or simpler than the proof of Theorem 2.2, we thus only prove Theorem 2.2. To prove Theorem 2.2, we proceed similarly as in the proof of [HT14a, Theorem 1]

Remark 2.2.

Looking back carefully at the proof of Theorem 2.2, we see that Theorem 2.2 is also valid if 𝚪=Γ2∪Γ4{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}=\Gamma_{2}\cup\Gamma_{4}. Moreover, we say that λ⁡(x,y)\lambda(x,y) satisfies the negative mm-condition if λ⁡(x,y)\lambda(x,y) satisfies (2.2) and the following condition:

where c0,c1c_{0},c_{1} are positive constants. Theorem 2.2 is also true if 𝚪{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}} is Γ1∪Γ4\Gamma_{1}\cup\Gamma_{4} or Γ2∪Γ3\Gamma_{2}\cup\Gamma_{3}, and λ⁡(x,y)\lambda(x,y) satisfies the negative mm-condition provided we choose properly the support of the mollifier.

3. The time dependent shallow water equations operator

In this section, we aim to study the semigroup property of the (modified) SWE operator (see below) with variable coefficients in the supercritical case on the Hilbert space ℋ𝚪m​(Ω)\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}(\Omega) (see (2.17a)) with 𝚪=Γ1∪Γ3{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}=\Gamma_{1}\cup\Gamma_{3}. We will successively consider the time-independent and the time-dependent cases. The linearized SWE operator that we consider reads

(3.1) 𝒜⁡(U^)​U=(u^​ux+v^​uy+g​ϕxu^​vx+v^​vy+g​ϕyu^​ϕx+v^​ϕy+ϕ^​(ux+vy)),\mathcal{A}(\widehat{U})U=\begin{pmatrix}\hat{u}u_{x}+\hat{v}u_{y}+g\phi_{x}\\ \hat{u}v_{x}+\hat{v}v_{y}+g\phi_{y}\\ \hat{u}\phi_{x}+\hat{v}\phi_{y}+\hat{\phi}(u_{x}+v_{y})\end{pmatrix},

where U^=(u^,v^,ϕ^)t,U=(u,v,ϕ)t\widehat{U}=(\hat{u},\hat{v},\hat{\phi})^{t},U=(u,v,\phi)^{t}; we set

ℰ1​(U^)=(u^0g0u^0ϕ^0u^),ℰ2​(U^)=(v^000v^g0ϕ^v^).\mathcal{E}_{1}(\widehat{U})=\begin{pmatrix}\hat{u}&0&g\\ 0&\hat{u}&0\\ \hat{\phi}&0&\hat{u}\end{pmatrix},\hskip 6.0pt\mathcal{E}_{2}(\widehat{U})=\begin{pmatrix}\hat{v}&0&0\\ 0&\hat{v}&g\\ 0&\hat{\phi}&\hat{v}\end{pmatrix}.

Note that ℰ1\mathcal{E}_{1}22 2 We sometimes write ℰ1=ℰ1​(U^)\mathcal{E}_{1}=\mathcal{E}_{1}(\widehat{U}) for the sake of conciseness, etc., ℰ2\mathcal{E}_{2} admit a symmetrizer S0=diag​(1,1,g/ϕ^)S_{0}=\text{diag}(1,1,g/\hat{\phi}), i.e. S0​ℰ1,S0​ℰ2S_{0}\mathcal{E}_{1},S_{0}\mathcal{E}_{2} are both symmetric. In order to take advantage of that, we consider the following modified SWE operator:

(3.2) 𝒜0​(U^)​U=ℰ10​(U^)​Ux+ℰ20​(U^)​Uy,\mathcal{A}^{0}(\widehat{U})U=\mathcal{E}_{1}^{0}(\widehat{U})U_{x}+\mathcal{E}_{2}^{0}(\widehat{U})U_{y},

where

ℰ10​(U^)=S01/2ℰ1(U^)S0−1/2=(u^0g​ϕ^0u^0g​ϕ^0u^),ℰ20​(U^)=S01/2ℰ2(U^)S0−1/2=(v^000v^g​ϕ^0g​ϕ^v^).\begin{split}\mathcal{E}_{1}^{0}(\widehat{U})&=S_{0}^{1/2}\mathcal{E}_{1}(\widehat{U})S_{0}^{-1/2}=\begin{pmatrix}\hat{u}&0&\sqrt{g\hat{\phi}}\\ 0&\hat{u}&0\\ \sqrt{g\hat{\phi}}&0&\hat{u}\end{pmatrix},\\ \mathcal{E}_{2}^{0}(\widehat{U})&=S_{0}^{1/2}\mathcal{E}_{2}(\widehat{U})S_{0}^{-1/2}=\begin{pmatrix}\hat{v}&0&0\\ 0&\hat{v}&\sqrt{g\hat{\phi}}\\ 0&\sqrt{g\hat{\phi}}&\hat{v}\end{pmatrix}.\end{split}

The reason why we choose the form (3.2) will become clear in the next section.

In the following, we assume that m≥3m\geq 3, the cases when m=0,1,2m=0,1,2 are similar or simpler. Here, we only consider the generic case when U^\widehat{U} does not vanish, and we first consider the time-independent case. We thus assume that U^\widehat{U} only depends on the space variables x,yx,y and that U^\widehat{U} satisfies the positive (m+1)(m+1)-condition (see (2.1)-(2.2)) introduced in Section 2, i.e.

(3.3) u^,v^,ϕ^​ satisfy the positive ​(m+1)​-condition;\hat{u},\hat{v},\hat{\phi}\text{ satisfy the positive }(m+1)\text{-condition};

the reason why we assume one more level of regularity on U^\widehat{U} will be explained below. As we indicated before, we only study the supercritical case, and we thus assume that U^\widehat{U} also satisfies the enhanced supercritical condition:

(3.4) u^2−g​ϕ^≥c22,v^2−g​ϕ^≥c22,\hat{u}^{2}-g\hat{\phi}\geq c_{2}^{2},\hskip 6.0pt\hat{v}^{2}-g\hat{\phi}\geq c_{2}^{2},

where c2c_{2} is a positive constant.

3.1. Boundary conditions

We aim to determine the boundary conditions which are suitable for the system

(3.5) 𝒜0​(U^)​U=ℰ10​(U^)​Ux+ℰ20​(U^)​Uy=F,\mathcal{A}^{0}(\widehat{U})U=\mathcal{E}_{1}^{0}(\widehat{U})U_{x}+\mathcal{E}_{2}^{0}(\widehat{U})U_{y}=F,

where F∈ℋ𝚪m​(Ω)3F\in\mathcal{H}^{m}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}(\Omega)^{3}. With assumption (3.4), we see that ℰ10\mathcal{E}_{1}^{0} and ℰ20\mathcal{E}_{2}^{0} are both positive definite. Thus, it is natural to treat either the xx- or yy-direction as the time-like direction. Let us choose the yy-direction, which means that we first need to specify the boundary conditions at y=0y=0 (time-like initial conditions); choosing the xx-direction would lead to the same result. Multiplying both sides of (3.5) by (ℰ20)−1(\mathcal{E}_{2}^{0})^{-1} gives

(3.6) Uy+ℰ20​(U^)−1​ℰ10​(U^)​Ux=ℰ20​(U^)−1​F.U_{y}+\mathcal{E}_{2}^{0}(\widehat{U})^{-1}\mathcal{E}_{1}^{0}(\widehat{U})U_{x}=\mathcal{E}_{2}^{0}(\widehat{U})^{-1}F.

We set κ0​(U^)=g⁡(u^2+v^2−g​ϕ^)/ϕ^\kappa_{0}(\widehat{U})=\sqrt{g(\hat{u}^{2}+\hat{v}^{2}-g\hat{\phi})/\hat{\phi}}, and we explicitly compute the eigenvalues of (ℰ20)−1​ℰ10(\mathcal{E}_{2}^{0})^{-1}\mathcal{E}_{1}^{0}:

(3.7) λ1=u^​v^+ϕ^​κ0v^2−g​ϕ^,λ2=u^​v^−ϕ^​κ0v^2−g​ϕ^,λ3=u^v^.\lambda_{1}=\frac{\hat{u}\hat{v}+\hat{\phi}\kappa_{0}}{\hat{v}^{2}-g\hat{\phi}},\hskip 6.0pt\lambda_{2}=\frac{\hat{u}\hat{v}-\hat{\phi}\kappa_{0}}{\hat{v}^{2}-g\hat{\phi}},\hskip 6.0pt\lambda_{3}=\frac{\hat{u}}{\hat{v}}.

Note that all the eigenvalues λ1,λ2,λ3\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3} of (ℰ20)−1​ℰ10(\mathcal{E}_{2}^{0})^{-1}\mathcal{E}_{1}^{0} are positive under assumption (3.4). Therefore, from the general hyperbolic theory (see Chapter 4 in [BS07]), it is necessary and sufficient to specify the boundary conditions for UU at x=0x=0 in order to solve (3.6) in UU.

In conclusion, in order to solve (3.5) in UU, we need to specify the boundary conditions for UU at x=0x=0 and y=0y=0. We then consider the homogeneous case and thus choose to specify the boundary conditions for UU:

(3.8) U=0, on 𝚪=Γ1∪Γ3={x=0}∪{y=0}.U=0,\text{ on }{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}=\Gamma_{1}\cup\Gamma_{3}=\{x=0\}\cup\{y=0\}.

As we will see in Lemma 3.2 and Section 5, any sufficiently regular solution UU for (3.5) and for the nonlinear equations (5.1) will satisfy the following compatibility boundary conditions:

(3.9) {∂kxU=0, on Γ1={x=0},∀ 0≤k≤m,∂kyU=0, on Γ3={y=0},∀ 0≤k≤m,\begin{cases}\partial^{k}_{x}U=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{1}=\{x=0\},\,\forall\,0\leq k\leq m,\\ \partial^{k}_{y}U=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{3}=\{y=0\},\,\forall\,0\leq k\leq m,\end{cases}

which, by differentiating with respect to the tangential direction, is equivalent to

(3.9′) ∂αU=0, on ​𝚪=Γ1∪Γ3,∀|α|≤m.\partial^{\alpha}U=0,\text{ on }{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}=\Gamma_{1}\cup\Gamma_{3},\,\forall\,|\alpha|\leq m.

Hence in the following, we use the compatibility boundary conditions (3.9) rather than the boundary conditions (3.8) for the domain of the unbounded operator AA defined below.

We write ℋ𝚪k=ℋ𝚪k​(Ω)3\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{k}=\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{k}(\Omega)^{3} for k≥0k\geq 0, in which the functions vanish on 𝚪\boldsymbol{\Gamma} (the part of the boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega), and we endow the space ℋ𝚪m\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m} with the Hilbert scalar product and norm of Hm​(Ω)3H^{m}(\Omega)^{3}:

⟨U,U¯⟩ℋ𝚪m=∑|α|≤m⟨∂αU,∂αU¯⟩L2​(Ω),∥U∥ℋ𝚪m={⟨U,U⟩ℋ𝚪m}1/2;\langle U,\overline{U}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}}=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq m}\langle\partial^{\alpha}U,\partial^{\alpha}\overline{U}\rangle_{L^{2}(\Omega)},\hskip 6.0pt\big\lVert U\big\rVert_{\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}}=\{\langle U,U\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}}\}^{1/2};

we then define the unbounded operator AA on ℋ𝚪m\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}, by setting A​U=𝒜0​(U^)​U,∀U∈𝒟⁡(A)AU=\mathcal{A}^{0}(\widehat{U})U,\,\forall U\in\mathcal{D}(A) and

𝒟⁡(A)={U∈ℋ𝚪m:𝒜0​(U^)​U=ℰ10​(U^)​Ux+ℰ20​(U^)​Uy∈ℋ𝚪m}.\mathcal{D}(A)=\{U\in\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}\,:\,\mathcal{A}^{0}(\widehat{U})U=\mathcal{E}_{1}^{0}(\widehat{U})U_{x}+\mathcal{E}_{2}^{0}(\widehat{U})U_{y}\in\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}\}.

Note that the compatibility boundary conditions (3.9) are already taken into account in the domain 𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{D}(A) (see also Propositions 2.4-2.5) since m≥3m\geq 3. We also introduce the corresponding smooth function space 𝒱⁡(Ω):=𝒱𝚪​(Ω)3\mathcal{V}(\Omega):=\mathcal{V}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}(\Omega)^{3}. Note that 𝒱⁡(Ω)\mathcal{V}(\Omega) is dense in ℋ𝚪m\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}, which is a direct consequence of Theorem 2.1. We also have the following results.

Lemma 3.1.

We assume that U^\widehat{U} satisfies the assumptions (3.3) and (3.4). Then:

    𝒱⁡(Ω)∩𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{V}(\Omega)\cap\mathcal{D}(A) is dense in 𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{D}(A).

    𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{D}(A) is dense in ℋ𝚪m\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}.

3.4. Semigroup

We now set B=ω0+AB=\omega_{0}+A, with 𝒟⁡(B)=𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{D}(B)=\mathcal{D}(A); then (B,𝒟⁡(B))(B,\mathcal{D}(B)) is a positive operator on ℋ𝚪m\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m} by virtue of (3.17), and ω+B\omega+B (=ω+ω0+A\omega+\omega_{0}+A) is surjective for all ω>0\omega>0 thanks to Lemma 3.2. Hence, Theorem A.1 (the Hille-Yosida theorem) implies that the operator −B-B generates a contraction semigroup on ℋ𝚪m\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}, and we then obtain the following result as a consequence of Theorem A.3 (Bounded Perturbation Theorem I).

Theorem 3.1.

The operator (−A,𝒟⁡(A))(-A,\mathcal{D}(A)) generates a quasi-contraction semigroup (R⁡(t))t≥0(R(t))_{t\geq 0} on ℋ𝚪m=ℋ𝚪m​(Ω)3\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}=\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}(\Omega)^{3} satisfying ∥R⁡(t)∥≤eω0​t,∀t≥0\big\lVert R(t)\big\rVert\leq e^{\omega_{0}t},\,\forall t\geq 0.

Remark 3.2.

The constant ω0\omega_{0} in Theorem 3.1 only depends on the HmH^{m}-norm of U^\widehat{U}.

In this subsection, we consider the case where U^\widehat{U} also depends on the time variable tt, and we impose the following assumptions on U^\widehat{U}:

Under these new assumptions, we see that the unbounded operator −A-A defined in Subsection 3.1 generates a strongly continuous semigroup with the same arguments as above, once we treat the time variable tt as a parameter. To be more precise, we define a family of unbounded operators A⁡(t)​UA(t)U on the Hilbert space HH with A⁡(t)​U=𝒜0​(U^​(t))​U,∀U∈𝒟⁡(A⁡(t)|H)A(t)U=\mathcal{A}^{0}(\widehat{U}(t))U,\,\forall U\in\mathcal{D}(A(t)|_{H}) and

where H=ℋ𝚪k(=ℋ𝚪k​(Ω)3)H=\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{k}(=\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{k}(\Omega)^{3}) and kk can be either m−1m-1, mm or m+1m+1.

Corollary 3.1.

The operators {−A⁡(t)}t\{-A(t)\}_{t} generate quasi-contraction semigroups (Rt,1​(s))s≥0(R_{t,1}(s))_{s\geq 0} on ℋ𝚪m−1\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m-1}, (Rt​(s))s≥0(R_{t}(s))_{s\geq 0} on ℋ𝚪m\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}, and (Rt,2​(s))s≥0(R_{t,2}(s))_{s\geq 0} on ℋ𝚪m+1\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m+1}, and they satisfy

Assume that U^\widehat{U} satisfies the assumptions (3.25a)-(3.25c) and m≥3m\geq 3. 4. The linear shallow water system

In this section, we aim to study the well-posedness of the linear shallow water system in certain Sobolev spaces using the evolution semigroups technique. Keeping the notations introduced in Section 3, the linear shallow water system reads in compact form

(4.1) Ut+ℰ1​(U^)​Ux+ℰ2​(U^)​Uy+ℓ⁡(U)=F,U_{t}+\mathcal{E}_{1}(\widehat{U})U_{x}+\mathcal{E}_{2}(\widehat{U})U_{y}+\ell(U)=F,

where ℓ⁡(U)=(−f​v,f​u,0)t\ell(U)=(-fv,fu,0)^{t}, and ff is the Coriolis parameter. Note that FF which does not appear in the linearized shallow water system (1.1) is added here for mathematical generality and also for the study of the non-homogeneous boundary conditions or for the nonlinear case. Observe that the system (4.1) is Friedrichs symmetrizable (see Chapter 1 in [BS07]) with symmetrizer S0=diag​(1,1,g/ϕ^)S_{0}=\text{diag}(1,1,g/\hat{\phi}), and in order to take advantage of that, we make as before a change of variables by setting U~=S012​U\widetilde{U}=S_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}U and substitute into (4.1); we obtain a new system for U~\widetilde{U} which reads

(4.2) U~t+𝒜0​(U^)​U~+ℬ⁡(U^)​U~=S012​F,\widetilde{U}_{t}+\mathcal{A}^{0}(\widehat{U})\widetilde{U}+\mathcal{B}(\widehat{U})\widetilde{U}=S_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}F,

where

(4.3) 𝒜0​(U^)​U~=ℰ10​(U^)​U~x+ℰ20​(U^)​U~y,ℬ⁡(U^)​U~=S012​((S0−12)t+ℰ1​(U^)​(S0−12)x+ℰ2​(U^)​(S0−12)y)​U~+ℓ⁡(U~).\begin{split}\mathcal{A}^{0}(\widehat{U})\widetilde{U}&=\mathcal{E}_{1}^{0}(\widehat{U})\widetilde{U}_{x}+\mathcal{E}_{2}^{0}(\widehat{U})\widetilde{U}_{y},\\ \mathcal{B}(\widehat{U})\widetilde{U}&=S_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}\big((S_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}})_{t}+\mathcal{E}_{1}(\widehat{U})(S_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}})_{x}+\mathcal{E}_{2}(\widehat{U})(S_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}})_{y}\big)\widetilde{U}+\ell(\widetilde{U}).\end{split}

If we now assume that U^\widehat{U} satisfies the conditions introduced in Subsection 3.5, then the family of operators {−A⁡(t)}t∈[0,T]\{-A(t)\}_{t\in[0,T]} satisfies the Kato-condition (see Lemma 3.3). If we further assume that U^\widehat{U} belongs to 𝒞⁡([0,T],Hm+2​(Ω))∩𝒞1​([0,T],Hm+1​(Ω))\mathcal{C}([0,T];H^{m+2}(\Omega))\cap\mathcal{C}^{1}([0,T];H^{m+1}(\Omega)), then the operators {B⁡(t)}t∈[0,T]\{B(t)\}_{t\in[0,T]} defined by B⁡(t)​U~=ℬ⁡(U^)​U~B(t)\widetilde{U}=\mathcal{B}(\widehat{U})\widetilde{U} are bounded operators on all the three spaces ℋ𝚪m−1,ℋ𝚪m,ℋ𝚪m+1\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m-1},\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m},\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m+1} by using the estimates in Lemma B.1. Therefore, with Theorem A.4 (Bounded Perturbation Theorem II), the family of operators {−A⁡(t)−B⁡(t)}t∈[0,T]\{-A(t)-B(t)\}_{t\in[0,T]} is a Kato-stable family, and furthermore, we have

Lemma 4.1.

The family {−A⁡(t)−B⁡(t)}t∈[0,T]\{-A(t)-B(t)\}_{t\in[0,T]} satisfies the Kato-condition with X=ℋ𝚪m−1X=\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m-1}, Y=ℋ𝚪mY=\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m} or X=ℋ𝚪mX=\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m}, Y=ℋ𝚪m+1Y=\mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^{m+1}.

Remark 4.3 (Non-homogeneous boundary conditions).

Using Remark 9.1 in [HT14a], the existence of a solution for the linear system (4.1) associated with non-homogeneous boundary conditions can be obtained, we omit the details here; see [RTT08b] for a similar situation.

5. The fully nonlinear shallow water system

In this section, we aim to investigate the well-posedness for Eqs. (1.1) associated with suitable initial conditions and homogeneous boundary conditions, and we will make a remark about the case of non-homogeneous boundary conditions. Keeping the notations introduced in Section 3 and 4, the fully nonlinear shallow water system reads in compact form

(5.1) Ut+ℰ1​(U)​Ux+ℰ2​(U)​Uy+ℓ⁡(U)=0.U_{t}+\mathcal{E}_{1}(U)U_{x}+\mathcal{E}_{2}(U)U_{y}+\ell(U)=0.

5.1. Stationary solution

We want to study system (5.1) near a stationary solution, and we start by constructing such a stationary solution (u,v,ϕ)=(us,vs,ϕs)(u,v,\phi)=(u_{s},v_{s},\phi_{s}). These functions are independent of time and satisfy

(5.2) ℰ1​(U)​Ux+ℰ2​(U)​Uy+ℓ⁡(U)=0.\mathcal{E}_{1}(U)U_{x}+\mathcal{E}_{2}(U)U_{y}+\ell(U)=0.

The existence of the general stationary solution UsU_{s} to (5.2), which satisfies the supercritical condition, is a 1-dimensional hyperbolic problem if we multiply by ℰ2−1\mathcal{E}_{2}^{-1} on both sides of (5.2) and treat the yy-direction as the time-like direction as we already did in Lemma 3.2. The general results in [BS07, Chapter 11] guarantee the existence of the stationary solution UsU_{s} if we specify suitable initial (yy-direction) and boundary (xx-direction) conditions. Actually, Subsection 2.1 in [HPT11] provides an yy-independent stationary solution to (5.2) satisfying the supercritical condition. But in what follows, we think of UsU_{s} in a general form (i.e. UsU_{s} depends both xx and yy).

We thus choose our stationary solution Us=(us,vs,ϕs)tU_{s}=(u_{s},v_{s},\phi_{s})^{t} of (5.2) satisfying a strong form of the supercritical condition, i.e.

(5.3) {2​c0≤us,vs,ϕs≤12​c1,us2−gϕs≥2c22,vs2−gϕs≥2c22,\begin{cases}2c_{0}\leq u_{s},v_{s},\phi_{s}\leq\frac{1}{2}c_{1},\\ u_{s}^{2}-g\phi_{s}\geq 2c_{2}^{2},\,v_{s}^{2}-g\phi_{s}\geq 2c_{2}^{2},\\ \end{cases}

where c0,c1,c2c_{0},c_{1},c_{2} are given, positive constants which will play the same role as those in (4.6).

We set U=Us+U~U=U_{s}+\widetilde{U}. Note that if we choose δ\delta sufficiently small so that if |U~|≤δ|\widetilde{U}|\leq\delta (i.e. |u~|,|v~|,|ϕ~|<δ|\tilde{u}|,|\tilde{v}|,|\tilde{\phi}|<\delta), then UU satisfies relations similar to (5.3), that is:

(5.4) {c0≤u~+us,v~+vs,ϕ~+ϕs≤c1,(u~+us)2−g(ϕ~+ϕs)≥c22,(v~+vs)2−g(ϕ~+ϕs)≥c22.\begin{cases}c_{0}\leq\tilde{u}+u_{s},\tilde{v}+v_{s},\tilde{\phi}+\phi_{s}\leq c_{1},\\ (\tilde{u}+u_{s})^{2}-g(\tilde{\phi}+\phi_{s})\geq c_{2}^{2},\,(\tilde{v}+v_{s})^{2}-g(\tilde{\phi}+\phi_{s})\geq c_{2}^{2}.\\ \end{cases}

The relations (5.4) will guarantee that we remain in the supercritical case.

We then substitute U=Us+U~U=U_{s}+\widetilde{U} into (5.1); we obtain a new system for U~\widetilde{U}, and dropping the tildes, our new system reads:

(5.5) Ut+ℰ1​(U+Us)​Ux+ℰ2​(U+Us)​Uy+ℓ⁡(U)=FU,U_{t}+\mathcal{E}_{1}(U+U_{s})U_{x}+\mathcal{E}_{2}(U+U_{s})U_{y}+\ell(U)=F^{U},

where

(5.6) FU=−ℰ1​(U+Us)​Us,x−ℰ2​(U+Us)​Us,y−ℓ⁡(Us)=(u​us,x+v​us,yu​vs,x+v​vs,yu​ϕs,x+v​ϕs,y+ϕ⁡(us,x+vs,y)).\begin{split}F^{U}&=-\mathcal{E}_{1}(U+U_{s})U_{s,x}-\mathcal{E}_{2}(U+U_{s})U_{s,y}-\ell(U_{s})\\ &=\begin{pmatrix}uu_{s,x}+vu_{s,y}\\ uv_{s,x}+vv_{s,y}\\ u\phi_{s,x}+v\phi_{s,y}+\phi(u_{s,x}+v_{s,y})\end{pmatrix}.\end{split}

In order to have the last equality, we use the fact that UsU_{s} is a stationary solution satisfying (5.2). We supplement (5.5) with the following initial and homogeneous boundary conditions:

Observe that we can rewrite (5.5) as

at x=0x=0, we immediately see that Ux|x=0=0U_{x}|_{x=0}=0. Remark 5.1 (Non-homogeneous boundary conditions).

With Remark 4.3, the existence of a solution for the iterative scheme (5.11) associated with non-homogeneous boundary conditions can be obtained, and by passing to the limit, the nonlinear system (5.5) associated with non-homogeneous boundary conditions admits a unique solution; we omit the details here.

Remark 5.2.

After completing this article, we found that we can also use a finite difference method to prove the existence and uniqueness of the fully nonlinear SWE (i.e. Theorem 5.1) by observing that we have the energy estimates (3.24) for the corresponding boundary value problem (although slightly different), which is the one we only need for the finite difference method. We omit the details here.

The finite difference method has the advantages that we do not need the density theorems in Section 2 and the evolution semigroup technique. However, the evolution semigroup technique has its own advantage that it tells us how we lost two space derivatives for the well-posedness of the linear SWE (see Theorem 4.1), and that explains why we only have local well-posedness for the fully nonlinear SWE in some sense.

Appendix A Preliminary results about semigroups and evolution families

This appendix collects some basic facts on the semigroups and evolution families and the characterization of their generators. The main references are the classical books by K. Yosida [Yos80], and by E. Hille and R.S. Phillips [HP74], and by A. Pazy [Paz83] and the book by K.-J. Engel and R. Nagel [EN00].

Definition A.1.

A family (S⁡(t))t≥0(S(t))_{t\geq 0} of bounded linear operators on a Banach space XX is called a strongly continuous (one-parameter) semigroup (or 𝒞0\mathcal{C}_{0}-semigroup) if it satisfies

  1. i)

    S⁡(0)=I,S⁡(t+s)=S⁡(t)​S​(s)S(0)=I,S(t+s)=S(t)S(s) for all t,s≥0t,s\geq 0;

  2. ii)

    ξx:t↦ξx​(t):=S⁡(t)​x\xi_{x}:t\mapsto\xi_{x}(t):=S(t)x is continuous from ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+} into XX for every x∈Xx\in X.

Proposition A.1.

For every strongly continuous semigroup (S⁡(t))t≥0(S(t))_{t\geq 0}, there exist constants ω∈ℝ\omega\in\mathbb{R} and M≥1M\geq 1 such that

(A.1) ∥S⁡(t)∥≤M​eω​t\big\lVert S(t)\big\rVert\leq Me^{\omega t}

for all t≥0t\geq 0.

Definition A.2.

A strongly continuous semigroup is called quasi-contraction if we can take M=1M=1 in (A.1), and called bounded if ω=0\omega=0, and called contraction if ω=0\omega=0 and M=1M=1 is possible.

Definition A.3.

The generator A:𝒟⁡(A)⊂X↦XA:\mathcal{D}(A)\subset X\mapsto X of a strongly continuous semigroup (S⁡(t))t≥0(S(t))_{t\geq 0} on a Banach space XX is the operator

A​x:=ξ˙x​(0)=limh↓01h​(S⁡(h)​x−x)Ax:=\dot{\xi}_{x}(0)=\lim_{h\downarrow 0}\frac{1}{h}(S(h)x-x)

defined for every xx in its domain

𝒟⁡(A):={x∈X:t↦ξx​(t)​ is right differentiable in ​t​ at ​t=0}.\mathcal{D}(A):=\{x\in X\,:\,t\mapsto\xi_{x}(t)\text{ is right differentiable in }t\text{ at }t=0\}.

Note that if ξx​(t)\xi_{x}(t) is right differentiable in tt at t=0t=0, it is also differentiable at tt, for any t≥0t\geq 0.

Theorem A.1 (Hille-Yosida theorem).

Let (A,𝒟⁡(A))(A,\mathcal{D}(A)) be a positive operator on a Hilbert space HH such that ω+A\omega+A is surjective for some ω>0\omega>0. Then −A-A generates a contraction semigroup.

We recall that on a Hilbert space, the linear operator AA is called positive if ⟨A​x,x⟩≥0\langle Ax,x\rangle\geq 0 for all x∈𝒟⁡(A)x\in\mathcal{D}(A).

Theorem A.2 (Uniqueness Theorem).

Let (A,𝒟⁡(A))(A,\mathcal{D}(A)) be a closed, densely defined operator on a Banach space XX, and let YY be a subspace of XX which is continuously embedded in XX (in symbols: Y↪XY\hookrightarrow X). The part of AA in YY is the operator A|A_{|} defined by A|​y:=A​yA_{|}y:=Ay with domain 𝒟⁡(A|)={y∈𝒟⁡(A)∩Y:A​y∈Y}\mathcal{D}(A_{|})=\{y\in\mathcal{D}(A)\cap Y:Ay\in Y\}. Suppose that (A,𝒟⁡(A))(A,\mathcal{D}(A)) generates a strongly continuous semigroup (S⁡(t))t≥0(S(t))_{t\geq 0} on XX, and (A|,𝒟⁡(A|))(A_{|},\mathcal{D}(A_{|})) also generates a strongly continuous semigroup (R⁡(t))t≥0(R(t))_{t\geq 0} on YY. Then

(A.2) S⁡(t)​y=R⁡(t)​yS(t)y=R(t)y

holds for all y∈Yy\in Y and t≥0t\geq 0. Furthermore, the subspace YY is AA-admissible, i.e. YY is an invariant subspace of S⁡(t),t≥0S(t),\,t\geq 0, and the restriction of S⁡(t)S(t) to YY, which is R⁡(t)R(t), is a strongly continuous semigroup on YY.

Proof.

The identity (A.2) immediately follows from the uniqueness of the following Cauchy problem

{u˙(t)=Au(t),∀t≥0,u⁡(0)=y∈Y;\begin{cases}\dot{u}(t)=Au(t),\,\forall\,t\geq 0,\\ u(0)=y\in Y;\end{cases}

and that YY is AA-admissible follows from (A.2) and the assumption.

∎

Theorem A.3 (Bounded Perturbation Theorem I).

Let (A,𝒟⁡(A))(A,\mathcal{D}(A)) be the infinitesimal generator of a strongly continuous semigroup (S⁡(t))t≥0(S(t))_{t\geq 0} on a Banach space XX satisfying

∥S⁡(t)∥≤M0​eω​t,∀t≥0,\big\lVert S(t)\big\rVert\leq M_{0}e^{\omega t},\,\forall\,t\geq 0,

where ω∈ℝ,M0≥1\omega\in\mathbb{R},M_{0}\geq 1. If B∈ℒ⁡(X)B\in\mathcal{L}(X), then C:=A+BC:=A+B, with 𝒟⁡(C):=𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{D}(C):=\mathcal{D}(A) generates a strongly continuous semigroup (R⁡(t))t≥0(R(t))_{t\geq 0} satisfying

∥R⁡(t)∥≤M0​e(ω+M0​∥B∥)​t,∀t≥0.\big\lVert R(t)\big\rVert\leq M_{0}e^{(\omega+M_{0}\big\lVert B\big\rVert)t},\,\forall\,t\geq 0.

The following results are taken from [Paz83, Chapter 5].

Definition A.4.

A two parameter family of bounded linear operators W⁡(t,s),0≤s≤t≤TW(t,s),0\leq s\leq t\leq T, on a Banach space XX is called an evolution system if the two following conditions are satisfied:

  1. i)

    W⁡(s,s)=I,W⁡(t,r)​W​(r,s)=W⁡(t,s)W(s,s)=I,W(t,r)W(r,s)=W(t,s) for 0≤s≤r≤t≤T0\leq s\leq r\leq t\leq T;

  2. ii)

    (t,s)↦W⁡(t,s)(t,s)\mapsto W(t,s) is strongly continuous for 0≤s≤t≤T0\leq s\leq t\leq T.

Let II be the interval [0,T][0,T], and (A⁡(t),𝒟​(A⁡(t))t∈ICLOSE(A(t),\mathcal{D}(A(t))_{t\in I} be the family of infinitesimal generators of strongly continuous semigroups St​(s),s≥0,S_{t}(s),s\geq 0, on a Banach space XX, and let YY be a Banach space which is densely and continuously embedded into XX. The following stability definition appeared in [Kat70, Kat73]:

Definition A.5 (Kato-stability and Kato-condition).

We say that the family {A⁡(t)}t∈I\{A(t)\}_{t\in I} is Kato-stable, if there exist constants M≥1M\geq 1 and ω∈ℝ\omega\in\mathbb{R} such that

∥Πj=1n​esj​A​(tj)∥≤M​eω​∑j=1nsj,\big\lVert\Pi_{j=1}^{n}e^{s_{j}A(t_{j})}\big\rVert\leq Me^{\omega\sum_{j=1}^{n}s_{j}},

holds for every time-ordered sequence (t1,⋯,tn)(t_{1},\cdots,t_{n}) in II and sj≥0s_{j}\geq 0; and we say that the family {A⁡(t)}t∈I\{A(t)\}_{t\in I} satisfies the Kato-condition on II if the following conditions are satisfied:

  1. i)

    {A⁡(t)}t∈I\{A(t)\}_{t\in I} is Kato-stable in XX.

  2. ii)

    YY is A⁡(t)A(t)-admissible for all t∈It\in I, and the family {A⁡(t)|Y}\{A(t)|_{Y}\} of the part of A⁡(t)A(t) in YY is Kato-stable in YY.

  3. iii)

    Y⊂𝒟⁡(A⁡(t))Y\subset\mathcal{D}(A(t)) holds for all t∈It\in I, and for all t∈It\in I, A⁡(t)A(t) is a bounded operator from YY into XX and the mapping t↦A⁡(t)t\mapsto A(t) is continuous in the ℒ⁡(Y,X)\mathcal{L}(Y,X) norm ∥⋅∥Y→X\big\lVert\cdot\big\rVert_{Y\rightarrow X}.

Remark A.1.

If for all t∈It\in I, A⁡(t)A(t) is the infinitesimal generator of a quasi-contraction (see Definition A.2) semigroup Rt​(s)R_{t}(s) satisfying ∥Rt​(s)∥≤eω​s\big\lVert R_{t}(s)\big\rVert\leq e^{\omega s}, then the family {A⁡(t)}t∈I\{A(t)\}_{t\in I} is clearly Kato-stable with constants M=1M=1 and ω\omega.

Theorem A.4 (Bounded Perturbation Theorem II).

Let {A⁡(t)}t∈I\{A(t)\}_{t\in I} be a Kato-stable family of infinitesimal generators with constants MM and ω\omega. Let {B⁡(t)}t∈I\{B(t)\}_{t\in I} be bounded linear operators on XX. If ∥B⁡(t)∥≤K\big\lVert B(t)\big\rVert\leq K for all t∈It\in I, then {A⁡(t)+B⁡(t)}t∈I\{A(t)+B(t)\}_{t\in I} is a Kato-stable family of infinitesimal generators with constants MM and ω+K​M\omega+KM.

Theorem A.5.

If the family {A⁡(t)}t∈I\{A(t)\}_{t\in I} satisfies the Kato-condition (see Definition A.5) then there exists a unique evolution system W⁡(t,s),0≤s≤t≤TW(t,s),0\leq s\leq t\leq T, in XX satisfying

Theorem A.6.
